title: Data centres face power curbs as regulator moves to protect grid
full_text:
Large data centres will be required to withstand disturbances on the electricity grid and have the capacity to rapidly reduce their power consumption, under new rules aimed at preventing the artificial-intelligence boom from threatening the reliability of Australia’s power supply.
The rule change by the Australian Energy Market Commission illustrates an attempt to reconcile the rise of artificial intelligence with concerns about the impact it has on the grid and the wider community.
The Albanese government has insisted it wants to attract billions of dollars in investment in AI infrastructure but it will also protect an electricity system already under pressure to meet rising demand, however data centre operators have warned increasing compliance costs are threatening investment into Australia.
The AEMC warned that data centres could create new risks for the national electricity market if large facilities automatically disconnected during disturbances, potentially worsening instability and affecting other electricity consumers.
The reforms will require large data centres and other inverter-based loads to remain connected through specified voltage and frequency disturbances, while imposing new requirements on larger electricity users to rapidly reduce consumption when required.
The move comes as the scale of data centre expansion gathers pace, with the Australian Energy Market Operator forecasting electricity consumption from the facilities will increase sevenfold over the next decade, from about 5 terawatt hours currently to 34 terawatt hours.
That would lift data centres’ share of operational demand across the National Electricity Market from about 3 per cent to 13 per cent, according to AEMO modelling.
The AEMC said the growth of cloud computing, artificial intelligence and other digital services was creating new challenges for the power system because large data centres relied heavily on inverter-based technology, which could respond rapidly to changes in grid conditions.
While the commission said there had not been a significant known system security incident caused by large loads in the NEM, it pointed to overseas events where disturbances had triggered sudden reductions in data centre demand, potentially compounding problems for electricity networks.
In Virginia, a transmission fault in July this year triggered two waves of data centre load loss totalling about 3800 megawatts.
In Ireland, a disturbance in May 2025 was associated with a 387MW reduction in data centre demand.
The commission warned that if multiple large facilities disconnected at the same time, the sudden loss of demand could worsen an initial disturbance and potentially contribute to wider disruption.
Under the new rules, loads with an inverter-based capacity of 30 megawatts or more will be classified as large and subject to strengthened technical access standards.
They will be required to remain connected through specified voltage and frequency disturbances and meet requirements for recovering their electricity consumption after an event. The rules also introduce requirements for detecting and responding to instability where a large load could contribute to problems on the network.
